Patient History
Attend to age, sex, hand dominance, current and prior occupations and avocations, prior
injury and disability, prior surgical procedures, and relevant comorbidities.
Equipment
Goniometer for accurate measure of angles
Dynamometer and thumb-pinch meter to assess grip and thumb strength.
Monofilaments or two-point discriminator for sensory examination
Doppler for vascular assessment, if available

General Physical Examination
The patient evaluation begins with a history, allowing the patient to recount his or her
understanding of the problem and detail other factors, such as location, exacerbating
and alleviating factors, and duration. General observation is helpful, noting any skin
changes; masses; erythema; swelling; and other discrete findings, such as nail pitting.
Observe active and passive motion and compare it to the opposite side. Next, a focused
motor and sensory examination is performed. It is helpful to evaluate the function of the
tendons actively and via the tenodesis effect. If the wrist is passively extended in a
cooperative and relaxed patient, obligate digital flexion should occur, with a preserved
digital cascade in which the little finger is flexed slightly more than the ring finger, which
is slightly flexed more than the long finger, and so on. The digits should point toward the
volar scaphoid tubercle. Assess for scissoring or rotational deformity. If the wrist is
passively flexed, the fingers should demonstrate obligate extension symmetrically. A
finger that remains flexed suggests extensor tendon pathology.
A brief motor and sensory examination is helpful for consultations in an urgent or
emergent setting. A gross motor examination involves testing thumb opposition
(median) and extension (radial) and abduction of the index finger via first dorsal
interosseous muscle (ulnar) strength. A basic sensory examination can be assessed at
the dorsal side of the thumb (radial nerve), the volar index distal phalanx (median nerve),
and the small finger (ulnar nerve). This brief examination documents the general status

For a more detailed motor examination, muscle groups must be isolated to evaluate the
function of the muscle or tendon of interest. For example, in evaluating the flexor
digitorum profundus (FDP) of the long finger, the hand is placed flat, palm up, on a table
while the little, ring, and index fingers are held flat and immobilized. To assess extensor
pollicis longus (EPL) function, the palm is placed flat on a table with the palm down, and
the patient is instructed to lift his or her thumb off the table.

Depending on the pathology, a more detailed sensory examination can incorporate two-
point discrimination testing for the radial and ulnar digital nerves. For a brief two-point
sensory test, the examiner places one or two points of the instrument perpendicular to
the patient’s hand, careful to apply consistent pressure and avoid skin blanching.
Sensation is recorded to the narrowest width at which the patient can correctly identify 7
of 10 correct responses. Normal two-point discrimination is expected to be 6 mm or less
in the volar aspect of the distal phalanx of the digits (Figure 2).
Figure 2 Clinical photograph shows two-point discrimination sensory testing. (Courtesy
of Suresh K. Nayar, MD, Baltimore, MD.)
If concern for vascular insufficiency or diminished pulses exists, Doppler, if accessible,
may be used to assess the radial and ulnar arteries at the wrist and the superficial
palmar arch and the radial/ulnar vascular bundles out to the distal phalanx.1
Several palpable and helpful surface landmarks are present in the hand and wrist. The
Lister tubercle on the dorsum of the radius is a reliable landmark to the dorsal approach
to the wrist. A soft spot approximately 1 cm directly distal to the Lister tubercle gains
access to the radiocarpal joint for wrist arthrocentesis and arthroscopy. On the volar
wrist and hand, by staying ulnar to the palmaris longus, surgeons may avoid injury to the
palmar cutaneous nerve and the median nerve and its motor branch. The radiocarpal
joint is approximately one fingerbreadth proximal to the distal flexion crease, which can
may helpful in planning incisions for distal radius fixation. The pisiform can be palpated
in the ulnar palm just distal to the wrist flexion crease. The hook of hamate is palpable

Overview
Compartments of the Hand
The hand contains 10 myofascial compartments:
Thenar compartment
The adductor pollicis acts as a single compartment.
Hypothenar compartment (may have multiple subcompartments)
Four dorsal and three volar interosseous muscle compartments
Carpal tunnel

Compartments of the Hand
Several compartments create closed spaces of the hand (Figure 3). Deep abscesses may
be contained within a single compartment but may spread with progression to other
compartments. For example, a thenar space abscess may present with localized swelling
and erythema, and pain may be present with thenar motor function (thumb opposition
or adduction).1,2
Compartment syndrome may be caused by multiple etiologies, including but not limited
to trauma/fracture, fluid extravasation, external pressure or compression, vascular
injury, and burns. The fascia that encases each compartment must be adequately
released to avoid muscle and neurovascular compromise. For example, complete
release of compartment syndrome of the hand may involve separate incisions releasing
the thenar, hypothenar, dorsal and volar interossei, carpal tunnel, and possibly digital
compartments.

Compartments of the Forearm
The dorsal or posterior compartment contains all extensor tendons. These include two
superficial, two intermediate, and five deep extensor tendons, all of which are
innervated by the posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) or radial nerve proper. The
superficial tendons include the extensor carpi ulnaris (ECU) and the anconeus. The
intermediate group includes all digital extensors (extensor digitorum and extensor digiti
minimi [EDM]) other than extensor indicis, which is in the deep compartment. In addition
to the extensor indicis, the deep compartment includes the supinator and all thumb
musculature (abductor pollicis longus [APL], EPL, extensor pollicis brevis [EPB]).

A careful study of origin, insertion, function, and innervation may help explain the basic
principles of tendon transfer. For example, in a low median nerve palsy (eg, motor

rerouted to augment thumb opposition. This tendon cannot be innervated by the
already injured nerve; in this case, the motor branch of the median nerve and its

common choice for tendon transfers because it has redundant function due to the
extensor digitorum communis (EDC) to the index finger. The tendon can be rerouted to
the volar side and attached to the abductor pollicis brevis (APB). The palmaris longus

Palmar Spaces of the Hand
Thenar Space
The thenar space is located dorsal to the index flexor tendons and volar to the adductor
pollicis fascia and the first dorsal interosseous fascia.
It is separated from the midpalmar space by the midpalmar septum, a fascial septum
extending from the palmar fascia to the long finger metacarpal. The thenar space is radial to
the septum.
Midpalmar Space
The midpalmar space is separated from the thenar space by the midpalmar septum. The
midpalmar space is ulnar to the septum.
The dorsal boundary of the midpalmar space is the fascia of the second and third volar
interosseous muscles; the volar boundary is formed by the flexor sheaths of the long, ring, and
little fingers and the palmar aponeurosis.
Hypothenar Space
The hypothenar space is located between the hypothenar septum and the hypothenar
musculature.
The dorsal boundary of the hypothenar space is the periosteum of the little finger metacarpal
and the deep hypothenar fascia; the volar boundary is formed by the palmar fascia and the
fascia of the superficial hypothenar muscles.
Radial Bursa
The radial bursa begins at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint and extends proximally to 1 to
2 cm proximal to the transverse carpal ligament.
Typically, the FPL sheath is continuous with the radial bursa.

Ulnar Bursa
The ulnar bursa begins at the proximal aspect of the little finger flexor sheath and extends 1 to
2 cm proximal to the transverse carpal ligament.
The synovial sheath of the little finger may connect with the ulnar bursa.
The Parona Space
The Parona space is located between the FDP tendon and the pronator quadratus fascia.
The Parona space facilitates communication between the radial and ulnar bursae.

Palmar Spaces of the Hand
Infection can localize to each of these potential spaces. For example, patients with a
midpalmar abscess may present with loss of palmar concavity and pain with middle and
ring finger motion. The space is approached via a volar incision. Infections involving the
Parona space may present as a horseshoe abscess because of the characteristic swelling
and involvement pattern observed. The space of Parona may connect the synovial
sheaths and the radial/ulnar bursa of the thumb and little finger/respectively; therefore,
the process may be horseshoe or U-shaped. In web space infections, termed collar
button abscesses, the abscess must be approached volarly and dorsally for adequate
débridement.
Fascial boundaries may restrict the spread of infection if managed early. Typically, small,
uncomplicated infections that can be approached via a dorsal approach can be managed
in the emergency department or at bedside via local anesthesia. Deeper, more extensile
infections that must be approached volarly may benefit from careful incision and
débridement, often in the operating room to avoid injury to the flexor tendons and the
neurovascular structures. Although clinical examination is adequate to diagnose the
condition in most settings, radiographs often are helpful to determine if any foreign
body or fracture is present and to evaluate grossly for bony changes that may suggest
osteomyelitis. Occasionally, ultrasonography, MRI, or CT with contrast may be useful in
delineating the extent of infection; however, typically, management is initiated based on
clinical findings rather than imaging studies, which often delay management and may

Osteology
The Digits
The bones of the finger are the proximal (P1), middle (P2), and distal (P3) phalanges.
The bones of the thumb are the proximal and distal phalanges.

The Digits
The proximal and middle phalanges are concave on their volar surface and convex
dorsally. Their articular base is concave, whereas their distal segments are convex and
round off into two convex knuckles. Similarly, the distal phalanx has a concave base but
has a widened distal tuft that supports the finger pulp and nail. Fractures of the phalanx
may be simple extra-articular fractures or more complex fractures involving the joint
surface.
Certain characteristic deformities can be appreciated in examining hand fractures. For
example, extra-articular base fractures of the proximal phalanx frequently fall into
hyperextension deformity (apex volar), resulting in loss of proximal interphalangeal (PIP)
joint extension. This is secondary from imbalance between the extrinsic extensor
tendons and the intrinsic extensor tendons.
More complex articular fractures may lead to dislocation. For example, fractures
involving a volar articular lip of the middle phalanx base may result in a dorsal fracture-
dislocation (PIP fracture-dislocation). On physical examination, difficulty with flexion, a
prominent middle phalanx base, crepitus with motion, and instability with radial and
ulnar deviation stress at the PIP joint may be noted. Even after reducing the PIP joint,
gross persistent instability may be noted on physical examination.

Fractures that consist of a large portion (>50%) of the articular surface may be unstable
with nonsurgical management and may be managed via plate and/or screw fixation or
external fixation; volar plate arthroplasty; or, in the chronic setting, articular
reconstruction with graft, such as a hemihamate autograft.7
To evaluate for rotational deformity, the digits may be examined end on, comparing
each digit to the adjacent one, and evaluated in as much digital flexion as possible, which
may magnify the deformity relative to the position of digital extension. When the MCP
and PIP joints are flexed, each digit should point toward the scaphoid tuberosity.
Rotational deformity may manifest as digital overlapping or gapping in between. Slight
overlap of the ring and small fingers may be normal; therefore, comparison with the
contralateral side is important.
Loss of active flexion can be quantified as the “tip to palm distance,” or can be
documented as “the patient lacks X amount of cm to the distal palmar crease in
attempted finger flexion.”
The Hand
The thumb carpometacarpal joint, or the trapeziometacarpal (TMC) joint, is biconcave-convex,
similar to two opposing saddles.
The TMC joint is primarily stabilized by the dorsal ligamentous complex—the dorsoradial
ligament and the posterior oblique ligament—and the deep anterior oblique ligament.
The multiple degrees of freedom confer a large arc of motion to the joint, which allows for the
complex interplay of motion at this joint.


The TMC joint allows for thumb opposition. Arthritis can be detected as crepitus and
pain with the so-called grind test, in which the examiner loads the joint with axial
pressure and makes circumduction and translational motions. With the lever test, the
base of the thumb metacarpal is gripped and then levered radially and ulnarly to the end

Distal Radius and Ulna
The distal radius articular surface has two concave facets, the scaphoid and lunate facets,
separated by the scapholunate, or anterior-posterior, ridge (Figure 5).
The sigmoid notch, along the ulnar border of the distal radius, is a shallow concavity for the
articulating ulnar head at the distal radioulnar joint.
The distal ulna is covered with hyaline cartilage on its dorsal, lateral, palmar, and distal
surfaces.
The ulnar styloid projects distally; at its base, the fovea is the origin of the distal radioulnar
ligaments.


Distal Radius and Ulna
The wrist can be conceptualized as three longitudinal columns: the radial column (radial
styloid and scaphoid fossa), the intermediate column (lunate fossa), and the ulnar
column (includes the articular disk). The distal radius articulates with the ulna at the
sigmoid notch. The so called column theory can clarify displacement and fixation
patterns for distal radius fractures and abutment syndromes, such as ulnar impaction
syndrome.
The differential diagnosis for radial-sided wrist pain is diverse, ranging from fracture and
tendinopathy to degenerative changes and ligamentous injury. In general, a distal to
proximal approach is undertaken in examining the wrist, starting from the thumb and
index carpometacarpal joints and moving proximal to the Lister tubercle, examining all
structures that fall in between.9
The differential diagnosis for atraumatic ulnar-side wrist pain includes but is not limited
to pathology of the articular disk or radioulnar ligaments, ulnar abutment syndrome,
ulnar neuropathy, and ECU tendinopathy. To confirm if wrist pain is ulnar in etiology, the
ulnocarpal stress test can be performed. For this test, the elbow is flexed to 90°, and the
wrist is maximally ulnarly deviated. The wrist is axially loaded and pronated/supinated in
an ulnarly deviated position. Pain indicates a positive test.10,11
Carpus
The carpus comprises eight small bones.
They traditionally are separated into two carpal rows: the proximal row, containing the
scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, and pisiform; and the distal row, containing the trapezium,
trapezoid, capitate, and hamate.
Scaphoid—The primary vascular supply is a branch of the radial artery at the dorsal ridge. A
group of smaller vessels enters the palmar tubercle and supplies the distal 30%. The
transverse carpal ligament attaches to the palmar tubercle.

Lunate—A dorsal and a palmar vascular supply are found in 80% of wrists; in 20% of wrists,
only a palmar supply is found. The lunate is broader palmarly than dorsally.
Triquetrum—The triquetrum articulates with the hamate distally, the lunate radially, and the
pisiform volarly. It is stabilized to the fovea of the ulna through the ulnotriquetral ligament.
Hamate—The hamate consists of the body and the hook (hamulus) of hamate, which serves
as an attachment for the transverse carpal ligament and for the origins of the flexor digiti
minimi and the opponens digiti minimi.
Capitate—The head (the proximal portion) often relies on a retrograde vascular supply. Two
ridges separate the distal articular surface into three facets for articulation with the
metacarpals of the index, long, and ring fingers.
Trapezoid—The trapezoid has two distal facets, which articulate with the metacarpal of the
index finger.
Trapezium—The trapezium has a saddle-shaped articulation with the base of the thumb
metacarpal. It also has a palmar groove for the FCR, bordered laterally by a palmar tuberosity
and the attachment for the transverse carpal ligament.
Pisiform—The pisiform is a sesamoid bone within the FCU tendon. It is the origin for the
abductor digiti minimi.

Carpus
The proximal carpal row, from radial to ulnar, contains the scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum,
and pisiform. The scaphoid is the most frequently fractured carpal bone, and its tenuous
blood supply with a watershed zone is proposed to contribute to a risk for nonunion.
Described as a twisted peanut, 75% of the surface of the scaphoid is articular cartilage.
The major blood supply of the scaphoid is the dorsal carpal branch, a branch from the
radial artery, providing approximately 80% via retrograde flow. Volarly, the superficial
palmar arch supplies the proximal 20%. The scaphoid tubercle and the distal pole can be
palpated just distal to the palmar wrist crease, and the proximal pole can be accessed
dorsally. Proximal pole fractures are prone to nonunion, and surgical management

The ulnar nerve arises from the medial cord of the brachial plexus (C8 through T1, ± C7; Figure

It passes from the posterior compartment of the brachium to the anterior compartment of the

The fibroosseous cubital tunnel is bordered by the ulnar groove of the medial epicondyle, a
fascial arcade spanning from the medial epicondyle to the olecranon that connects the

superficially, radial to the FCU tendon.
The ulnar nerve lies ulnar (medial) and dorsal to the ulnar artery.
The dorsal sensory branch divides from the ulnar nerve approximately 5 cm proximal to the
wrist.
At the wrist, the ulnar nerve is 45% motor and 55% sensory.
Ulnar nerve topography is well known. In the proximal forearm, sensory fascicles controlling
palmar ring and little finger sensation are found on the radial side of the ulnar nerve. The deep

located dorsally and ulnarly.19

bifurcation, approximately 1 cm distal to the pisiform. It lies dorsal to the volar carpal
ligament and volar to the transverse carpal ligament. The ulnar artery bifurcates distal to the

The ulnar nerve innervates the FCU, FDP (ring and small finger), and most of the intrinsic

Anatomy of the Skin and Fascia
The anatomy of the palmar and digital fascia is relevant to Dupuytren disease, a benign
heritable fascial-proliferative disorder characterized by thickening and contractures
(implicating myofibroblasts) of the palmar fascia. In this disease, tethering of the palmar
surface that forms pits, nodules, and cords may result in fixed flexion contractures of the
MCP, PIP, and/or DIP joints.
In Dupuytren disease, normal fascial bands may turn into pathologic cords at the
palmar, palmodigital, and digital levels. The most notable cords are the spiral, central,
retrovascular, and natatory cords. Spiral cords cause PIP joint flexion contracture,
originating from pretendinous and spiral bands that insert onto the Grayson ligament
and the lateral digital sheet. Spiral cords can displace the neurovascular bundles
centrally and palmarly, placing the neurovascular bundle at risk during fasciectomy.
Central cords cause MCP joint flexion contracture, and retrovascular cords are
responsible for DIP joint flexion contracture. Finally, natatory cords can cause web space
contracture.

In the fingers, the MCP joint is a triaxial condyloid joint. The typical range of motion is from
15° of hyperextension to 90° of flexion. The trapezoidal shape of the metacarpal head
creates a cam effect on the collateral ligaments, causing the ligaments to be taut during MCP
joint flexion and lax during extension. Therefore, the MCP joint is stable in flexion and
unstable in extension.
In the thumb, dissimilar from in the fingers, the metacarpal head is a single broad condyle.
Sesamoids are contained within the volar plate. The thumb MCP joint varies widely in normal
range of motion. The ulnar collateral ligament includes proper and accessory portions. The
proper collateral extends from the proximal phalanx to the metacarpal head, whereas the
accessory collateral originates on the metacarpal head and inserts into the volar plate.
The PIP joint
The PIP joint is a hinge joint. The head of the proximal phalanx includes two condyles
separated by an intercondylar notch. This notch provides some inherent joint stability
through its articulation with the median ridge at the base of the middle phalanx.
The collateral ligaments at the PIP joint are taut throughout range of motion.
Proper collateral ligament—The origin is at the pit on the head of the proximal phalanx; the
ligament inserts into the lateral tubercle of the base of the middle phalanx.
Accessory collateral ligament—Also originates at the pit of the head of the proximal
phalanx but just volar to the proper collateral ligament. Inserts into the volar plate
Volar plate—A thick, fibrocartilaginous floor that originates within the A2 pulley and inserts
into the rough area at the base of P2. The volar plate supports the insertion of the
accessory collateral ligament and prevents PIP joint hyperextension.
The DIP joint—The DIP joint is stabilized by the collateral ligaments, the terminal extensor
tendon insertion, the FDP insertion, and the volar plate.

Central slip insufficiency (boutonnière deformity) and sagittal band insufficiency are two
commonly encountered pathologies of the extensor apparatus. Both can occur with
rheumatoid arthritis; however, with modern medications, synovitis severe and
prolonged enough to cause these issues is unusual. In boutonnière deformity, the MCP
and DIP joints are extended as the PIP joint is flexed.33 In traumatic boutonnière
deformity, the central slip is ruptured, resulting in loss of PIP joint extension. Over time,
the triangular ligament will attenuate, and the lack of suspension will cause the lateral
bands to drift palmar. In this position the lumbricals act to flex the PIP joint. Finally, the
palmar migration of the lateral bands will further flex the PIP joint and hyperextend the
DIP joint because of their insertion point on the distal phalanx. In a traumatic central
slip, initial injury may be missed because the intact lateral bands can provide PIP joint
extension before they eventually migrate palmarly.
The Elson test can be used to evaluate for extensor tendon injury at the central slip. In
this test, the PIP joint is flexed to 90°, often placed over the edge of a table. The patient
is asked to extend their PIP joint against resistance. Weak PIP joint extension with the
DIP joint strongly extending or hyperextending is suggestive of central slip injury (Figure
18).
In sagittal band rupture, the extensor tendon subluxates, usually ulnarward. Extensor
subluxation can be visualized during MCP joint extension and is experienced as a
snapping-type sensation. In a sagittal band rupture, patients are unable to actively
extend their MCP joint but can hold the finger in extension after passively extended. This
assessment can differentiate from other causes of diminished MCP joint extension, such
as PIN palsy.

Ligaments
The ligamentous network of the wrist may appear complicated. Extrinsic and intrinsic
wrist ligaments are present. The intrinsic ligaments bridge carpal bones together,
whereas the extrinsic ligaments bridge the carpus to the radius and ulna, hence the
terms intrinsic and extrinsic to the carpus.
The most important extrinsic volar ligaments, from radial to ulnar, are the
radioscaphocapitate (extends from the radial styloid and inserts onto the capitate,
serving as a sling for the scaphoid), long radiolunate, and short radiolunate. The
radioscaphocapitate ligament becomes the primary stabilizer of the wrist after a
proximal row carpectomy and prevents the capitate from drifting ulnarly. It can be
clearly observed after scaphoid carpectomy and must be preserved in its entirety. The
long and short radiolunate ligaments stabilize the lunate. Although their importance is a
subject of debate, the two most important dorsal ligaments are the dorsal intercarpal
ligament (spans the scaphoid to the triquetrum) and the dorsal radiotriquetal ligament
(spans the radius to the triquetrum).

Triangular Fibrocartilage Complex
The triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) refers to a conceptual group of related anatomic
structures; however, their interrelatedness is a subject of debate.
The structures included are the dorsal and volar radioulnar ligaments, the articular disk
between them, the meniscal homologue, the floor of the ECU tendon sheath, and the volar
ulnocarpal ligaments (Figure 19).
The meniscal homologue is a complex fibrocartilaginous structure that forms part of the ulnar
collateral ligament complex of the wrist. It provides structural and suspensory support. The
homologue originates from the ulnar styloid, converges into the ulnar collateral ligament, and
inserts onto the triquetrum and hamate distally.
The dorsal and volar radioulnar ligaments are the primary stabilizers of the distal radioulnar
joint. They originate from the base of the ulnar styloid and insert onto the dorsal and volar
margins of the sigmoid notch of the radius.
A separate deep portion of the origin of the distal radioulnar ligaments (the ligamentum
subcruentum) may be important. This is a subject of debate.
Only the peripheral 10% to 40% of the volar, ulnar, and dorsal articular disk has a vascular
supply.

Carpal Kinematics
The proximal carpal row has no muscular or tendinous attachments and is an intercalary
segment.
With ulnar deviation, the proximal row extends relative to the forearm/distal row. With radial
deviation, the proximal row flexes relative to the forearm/distal row.
With axial loading through the neutral wrist, approximately 80% of forces are transmitted
through the distal radius (60% scaphoid facet, 40% lunate facet) and 20% through the distal
ulna.
With wrist flexion, 60% of the motion is midcarpal and 40% is radiocarpal. With wrist
extension, 33% of the motion is midcarpal and 66% is radiocarpal.

Alternative schools of thought explain carpal kinematics, which are not completely
understood. In the link concept, motion is transmitted through the radius, lunate, and
capitate, with the lunate acting as an intercalated segment and the capitate serving as
the center of motion. In the row concept, the scaphoid serves as a bridge between the
proximal and distal carpal row. In this concept, motion occurs within and between each
row. In the column concept, three separate centers of motion are present between the
lateral (scaphoid, trapezoid, and trapezium), central (lunate, capitate, and hamate), and
medial (triquetrum) carpal segments. In this concept, the scaphoid and lunocapitate
articulation are the centers of motion for the medial and center columns, whereas the
triquetrum articulates with the entire distal row. Additional current tests assessing
complex wrist motion, such as the dart thrower arc, show that radiocarpal motion is
relatively limited compared with midcarpal motion.38

The Hand
The intrinsic musculature of the hand is a complicated system that allows for dexterous,
coordinated movement. The dorsal (four) and volar (three) interossei work with the
lumbricals to flex the MCP joints and extend the PIP/DIP joints. The dorsal interossei also
provide digital abduction, and the volar interossei adduct the fingers.
Conversely, intrinsic minus, or claw hand, is the opposite of intrinsic plus. In this
position, the hand assumes the opposite position of intrinsic motor function. Instead,
the MCP joints are hyperextended and the PIP/DIP joints are flexed. This deformity may
be secondary to an ulnar (cubital or ulnar tunnel) neuropathy or Volkmann ischemic
contracture. This condition generally requires contracture release and/or tendon
transfer.

Standard
Volar Approach to the Flexor Tendons
This approach is indicated for exploration and repair of the flexor tendons, the digital
neurovascular bundle, infection (eg, flexor tenosynovitis), palmar fascia excision for Dupuytren

The finger is flexed, and the dorsal margin of the interphalangeal flexion creases are marked

The volar approach to the distal radius has been the mainstay for distal radius fractures since

edges of the pronator quadratus are raised sharply off the bone, and then the muscle is

pronator quadratus is optional because does not appear to be helpful. 49

An appropriate-length incision is centered over the Lister tubercle or in line with the long
metacarpal. After the distal radius is exposed, the extensor retinaculum is opened over the
EPL, and the EPL tendon is mobilized and transposed radially, the location at which it is left
subcutaneously at the end of the procedure. The dorsal wrist often is exposed by elevating the
fourth compartment subperiosteally but leaving the compartment intact. An alternative is to
step-cut the retinaculum of the fourth compartment, allowing for later repair. This exposes the
fourth compartment tendons, which may be retracted aside. Deep to the fourth compartment,
the PIN will lie on the dorsal surface of the distal radius. Occasionally, PIN neurectomy is
performed based on the assumption that it will reduce pain. At this level, additional dissection
can be carried proximally or distally as necessary. To access the carpus distally, a simple
longitudinal capsular incision is made and later repaired at the end of the procedure.
Ulnar Approach to the Distal Ulna
The distal ulna is a subcutaneous structure that can be readily accessed via an ulnar-based
incision, with dissection carried between the FCU and the ECU. Dorsal sensory branches of the
ulnar nerve may be encountered. The ulna is exposed, and the ulnar origin of the extensor
retinaculum may be elevated as necessary.55
Volar Approach to the Scaphoid
The scaphoid can be approached volarly for reduction and internal fixation or
nonunion.56, 57,58

If necessary, the volar approach to the scaphoid can be carried as an extension from the
modified Henry or volar approach to the distal radius. An oblique, often zigzag, incision can be
made so that the wrist flexion crease is not crossed longitudinally, avoiding any subsequent
scar contracture.
If used as a primary approach, the incision is centered over the scaphoid tubercle and carried
proximally and distally in line with the FCR tendon. The superficial palmar branch of the radial
artery crosses the distal aspect of the wound. Although this branch typically is ligated, an
attempt may be made to mobilize and retract it. The FCR tendon sheath is divided as distal as
possible, and the tendon is retracted ulnarly. Deep, the volar wrist ligaments
(radioscaphocapitate and long radiolunate ligaments) are transected obliquely, in line with the
thumb metacarpal and the scaphoid, starting on the distal pole of the scaphoid. An attempt is
made to repair these ligaments. The volar ligaments are strongly adherent to the scaphoid,
and sharp dissection is necessary to elevate full-thickness flaps from the scaphoid. Placement
a needle in what is thought to be the fracture and confirming location on imaging studies
before performing drilling or cutting is beneficial.
Dorsal Approach to the Scaphoid
The dorsal approach to the scaphoid affords access to the proximal pole and the scapholunate
interval.59 This approach is an extension of the dorsal approach to the wrist. A 4-cm
longitudinal incision is made, starting at the Lister tubercle and extended distally. The
superficial branch of the radial nerve may be encountered radially. The extensor retinaculum
is then incised in line with the EPL, which is retracted radially along with the second extensor
compartment. The dorsal wrist ligaments are then incised in a T-type capsulotomy, starting at
the distal margin of the dorsal distal radius and ending just proximal to the dorsal intercarpal
ligament to expose the proximal pole of the scaphoid. Flexing the wrist helps deliver the
proximal pole to the surgical window.
Mini-open approaches have been described, with theoretic advantages of avoiding extensor
tendon and capsular dissection and preserving vascular supply and obtaining a more direct
starting point for screw fixation.60

The open carpal tunnel approach is made in line with the radial border of the ring finger.61 The
incision is carried approximately from the distal wrist flexion crease to the Kaplan cardinal line.
An effective release can be made via an approximately 2.5-cm incision. After dissecting
through the subcutaneous fat and incising the palmar fascia, the transverse carpal ligament
can be observed as a band of transverse fibers. Incising the ligament near the radial border of
the hook of hamate may help limit the potential for injury to the motor branch of the median
nerve. More thenar muscle belly on the ligament than usual is suggestive of a
transligamentous motor branch.
